The wrong pair is (2) Tadoba – Rock-cut Caves.

The chapter lists Tadoba, along with Dajipur and Sagareshwar, among the sanctuaries of Maharashtra, not among the rock-cut caves. The rock-cut caves it names are those at Ajanta, Verul and Gharapuri (Elephanta).

The other three pairs are correct: Matheran is listed among the hill stations, Kolhapur among the pilgrim centres, and Ajanta is a World Heritage site.

Tourism has become an independent field of local, interstate, national and international business, and several kinds of tourism bring people to and from India in large numbers.

People from western countries find the health services and facilities in India comparatively cheaper, and come to India to avail of the medical facilities and health services. India is a tropical country with ample sunlight throughout the year, which attracts tourists from countries with a cold climate, and the availability of Yoga training and of therapies based on Ayurveda is one more reason for them to visit.

Travel also goes the other way. Indian farmers now visit faraway places such as agricultural research centres, agricultural universities and countries like Israel, where experimentation in advanced agricultural technology is carried out.

Because of reasons like these, the number of people travelling back and forth from India has increased considerably.

It is a hard task to preserve and conserve heritage sites, and damage done to them cannot be undone.

The chapter says that a few things must be avoided at any instance — vandalising or defacing heritage monuments and sites. Everybody should therefore refrain from activities like writing on walls, carving on trees or painting ancient monuments in garish colours. Lack of good amenities in the precincts of heritage sites causes filthiness.

These are simple, primary precautions that every visitor can take, and taking them is what keeps a site fit to be visited, which is why they matter so much for preserving historical heritage sites.

The tradition of travelling is quite old in India. People used to travel for various reasons — pilgrimage, going to local fairs and festivals, the search for a renowned teacher and good education, and trade. In brief, from ancient times people took to travelling for various reasons.

Buddhist literature tells us that Gautam Buddha travelled to several cities in ancient India for preaching, and Buddhist monks were ordained not to stay at one place but to keep travelling continuously; Jain monks and sadhus also travelled constantly. Yuan Shwang, the Chinese monk, travelled to India in 630 C.E., and in the medieval period Saint Namdev, Saint Eknath, Guru Nanak and Ramdas Swami travelled extensively in India.

Tourism itself can be defined as travelling to visit places in distant regions for a specific purpose.

Marco Polo was an Italian traveller of the 13th century.

He introduced Asia, and especially China, to Europe. He stayed in China for 17 years, and he wrote about the flora and fauna, the social life, the culture and the trade systems of Asia.

His accounts belong with those of the other travellers the chapter names — Benjamin of Tudela, known as the first European traveller, and Ibn Batuta of the 14th century — whose writings are valuable historical documents.

Agro-tourism, also known as agri-tourism, is a rapidly developing type of tourism.

It is especially meant for the urban population, which has very little exposure to rural life and to agriculture, and it gives them that exposure directly.

The traffic also runs the other way: Indian farmers now visit faraway places such as agricultural research centres, agricultural universities and countries like Israel, where experimentation in advanced technology of agriculture is carried out.

The crucial issue in the development of tourism is providing proper guidance to national and international tourists — about the various aspects of the actual travel, about proper social conduct during the tour and about their stay at the destination places.

Along with that, several things are of great significance in promoting tourism: giving priority to safe transport and security facilities for tourists, amenities of a reasonably good standard, the availability of good accommodation and good washroom facilities on the travel routes. It is also very important to pay special attention to the special needs of handicapped tourists.

Preserving the sites themselves is a further issue. Vandalising or defacing heritage monuments must be avoided, and a lack of good amenities in the precincts of heritage sites causes filthiness. Pamphlets, guides and history material are also essential for tourists.

The question refers to the local people at a tourist centre such as Mahabaleshwar or Panchagani, where thousands of tourists arrive.

Those tourists are accompanied by guides who provide relevant information on the sightseeing tour. At some places photographers are present to click nice snaps for the tourists, and horsekeepers provide horses for horse rides and horse cart rides. It is the local people who are engaged in all these activities, and they can earn good money for their services.

More generally, markets in the vicinity grow along with the development of a tourist centre, so local handicrafts and cottage industries also begin to develop and the demand for locally processed food items and ethnic handicrafts increases, which results in better income for local artisans, business people and wage earners. In short, tourism becomes a major source of their livelihood.

The chapter names the things a place needs if tourism is to grow there, and these can be applied to one's own village or town.

First, visitors need proper guidance about the travel, about proper social conduct during the tour and about their stay, so trained local guides and clear pamphlets and history material about the local monuments should be prepared. Second, priority should be given to safe transport and security for tourists, to amenities of a reasonably good standard, to good accommodation and to good washroom facilities on the travel routes, with special attention to the needs of handicapped tourists.

The historical places nearby should be protected from vandalism and defacement — no writing on walls, no carving on trees, no painting of ancient monuments in garish colours — and good amenities should be provided in their precincts so that they do not become filthy. 'Heritage Walks' can be organised to the historical places of the area, which also encourages people to support conservation and to collect and publish authentic information about them.

As the tourist centre develops, local markets, handicrafts and cottage industries grow with it, so local artisans and businesses should be helped to offer locally processed food items and ethnic handicrafts.

[Note: this question asks the student for their own suggestions, so the points above are the measures the chapter itself names as important for the growth of tourism.]

World Heritage Sites

- Rock-cut Caves → the rock-cut caves at Ajanta, Verul and Gharapuri (Elephanta)
- Natural Heritage → Kas Plateau in Maharashtra, located in the Western Ghats, which is a World Natural Heritage site
- Railway Station → Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Railway Terminus in Maharashtra
- Sanctuary → The chapter does not state this.

The chapter also names the Taj Mahal at Agra and the Jantar Mantar observatory at Jaipur among the globally acclaimed Heritage Sites of India, and it divides the heritage of any country into Natural Heritage and Cultural (manmade) Heritage.

[Note: the chapter names sanctuaries at Dajipur, Sagareshwar and Tadoba as important tourist centres in Maharashtra, but it does not say that any sanctuary is a World Heritage Site, so that cell cannot be filled from this chapter.]

Tourism and Hospitality is an industry with the potential to create the maximum employment opportunities, and if managed professionally it is a very stable industry with tremendous scope for experimentation and innovation.

A tourist destination begins to receive revenue even before the tourist arrives at its airport, because he has to pay for his visa. He then spends on travel, on his stay in hotels, on food, on payments to translators and guides, and on buying newspapers, reference books and souvenirs, all of which contributes to the growth of that country's economy.

Markets in the vicinity grow along with the development of a tourist centre, so local handicrafts and cottage industries develop too and the demand for locally processed food items and ethnic handicrafts increases, giving better income to local artisans, business people and wage earners.

Guiding is a field in its own right: guides provide relevant information on the sightseeing tour, photographers work at tourist places, and horsekeepers provide horse rides and horse cart rides. 'Heritage Walks' — organised tours to visit historical places — have become popular as a group activity in many countries and are organised regularly in Ahmedabad, Mumbai and Pune; they also encourage work in the conservation and preservation of historical monuments and in collecting and publishing authentic information about them.

Geographic Tourism: this involves visiting places to observe the special geographic features of a region. It includes natural and animal sanctuaries, places such as the valley of flowers in Uttarakhand, various beaches, and unique geographical wonders like the crater lake at Lonar and the ranjankhalage — naturally carved out cavities in rocks — at Nighoj in Maharashtra. Many tourists visit these places to satisfy their curiosity.

Health Tourism: people from western countries find the health services and facilities in India comparatively cheaper, and come to India to avail of its medical facilities and health services. India is a tropical country with ample sunlight throughout the year, which attracts tourists from cold countries, and the availability of Yoga training and of Ayurveda-based therapies is one more reason to visit.

Agro-Tourism: also known as agri-tourism, this is rapidly developing and is especially meant for the urban population, which has very little exposure to rural life and agriculture. Indian farmers in turn now travel to agricultural research centres, agricultural universities and countries like Israel, where advanced agricultural technology is being tried out.

[The chapter also describes Sports Tourism, which developed in the 20th century around international events such as the Olympics, Wimbledon, the World Chess Championship and international cricket tournaments.]
